Remote work’s productivity effect is contested: some studies find remote work more productive, while others find it less productive than office work. Evidence includes reports of 5–9% higher remote efficiency and longer workdays [d1], employer surveys showing productivity was the same or higher under remote/hybrid arrangements [d4], and Gallup estimates of a 15% productivity bump for engaged remote workers [d6]. Conversely, calibrated models and expert statements assert office work is always more productive [d2], and major research programs associate fully remote work with 10–20% lower productivity than fully in-person work [d11]. Long-run studies highlight reduced learning and feedback in remote settings, implying productivity disadvantages over time [d10].
